Christ reached us as the Word - his own speech, the good news, carried in Scripture and preached, not invented by us or discovered freshly on our own. Our founder said plainly: I did nothing; the Word did it all. We do not claim an eyewitness chain back to his own days - more than fourteen hundred years lie between his time and ours - but what we have is his promise, and our confession of what that promise says.

Every household under our catechism said the same words each week: I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. Not one or the other - both together, in the same breath. He redeemed us, a lost and condemned people, and bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power - not with gold or silver, but with his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. On the third day he rose again from death, lives and reigns forever. That confession is what we have. We did not argue it the way a historian weighs evidence. We confessed it.

And each of us said this too: He is my Lord. That claim was not private in the way your own era might hear it - it was said by a whole household together, the same words on every tongue - but it was not distant either. Each person's own mouth said my Lord, not only our Lord.

What reached us of Jesus was the Word - his own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture. We did not invent it and we did not discover it freshly ourselves; it reached us the way the Word always reaches anyone, our founder says: preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. Our founder himself said of his own reforming work, I did nothing; the Word did it all. Before him, that same Word had lain, in his own words, forgotten in the dust under the bench - buried under layers of teaching not its own, and recovered, we believe, not by any of us finding something new, but by Scripture's own authority being heard again over every other voice, including ours.

By what path did it arrive? Not through a living chain of witnesses we ourselves could name. More than fourteen hundred years lie between his days and ours, and nothing in our record claims an unbroken line of hands laid on heads back to that time. What we claimed instead was agreement - that in what we teach and how we worship, nothing has been received on our part against Scripture or against the ancient, universal Church. We took the greatest care, we said, to keep new and godless teaching out, not to bring anything new in. But the path itself, witness by witness, generation by generation, is not something our own record traces step by step. What we have is the Word itself, and our own confession of what it says.

We would speak to you first about what believing itself is, and where it comes from. Believing, for us, is not a thing a person manufactures in themselves - it is trust that clings to a promise spoken from outside, and it is conceived from hearing the Word, not produced by our own effort. The Word did it all, our founder said plainly - preached, printed, taught, not argued into being by anyone's own work. So the first thing we would say to your trouble is this: you are not being asked to produce something you do not have. You are being asked to hear something already spoken.

What did we have of Jesus ourselves? The Word - his own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture. We did not discover it freshly on our own, and we do not pretend any of us knew someone who saw him; more than fourteen hundred years lie between his days and ours, and nothing in our record claims a living chain of witnesses back to that time. What we have is the Word itself, and our own confession of what it says. Each week, every household under our catechism said the same words: I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary - conceived by the Holy Spirit, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried, and on the third day rose again from the dead. That confession is what we have. We do not argue the resurrection the way a historian weighs evidence; we confess it.

Christ alone is our one teacher and our one mediator. We do not listen to saints or scholars instead of him; every page of Scripture points to him. The promise he speaks is this: that he redeemed us - a lost and condemned people - and bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power, not with gold or silver but with his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. And each of us says, in the very next breath, He is my Lord - I am his very own.

We would not tell you that believing is easy, or that trouble with it is rare. Our own founder complained, more than once, that even those who heard the Gospel held it too lightly, and at his own table someone asked him why we prayed so cold and careless under the new teaching while others had prayed with such vehemence under the old. Cold hearts were not strangers to us; they were among us, named plainly. What we hold against that coldness is not a method for producing warmth, but the Word itself, carried to the ears where it can be heard, and the promise spoken as though from God himself: given for you. The hearing itself is the Holy Spirit's own work, not ours - we cannot get farther than another person's ears.

So: you say you cannot manage to believe. We would ask you to hear the Word - Christ alone, the one Mediator, the one who stands between us and God on our behalf. We would not tell you to manufacture trust where you have none. We would tell you what the promise says, and trust that the Word must do it.

We confessed that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. Not one or the other -- both, in the same breath, said by the same mouth. Every household under our catechism said this each week: I believe in Jesus Christ, God's only Son, our Lord.

We did not settle this ourselves, as though it were a question we put to a vote. The confession that Christ is truly God is something we received, already settled, centuries before our founder was born, and we confessed it as inherited teaching. What we have is the confession itself, said -- not an argument we built from first principles to prove it.

Christ alone is our one Mediator, our one High Priest, the one who stands between us and God on our behalf -- no saint, no teacher, no priest of our own beside him. He redeemed us with his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. The catechism even lets each believer say this in their own voice: He is my Lord! I am his very own. That claim is not private in the way your phrase "personal Lord and Savior" might mean -- it is said by a whole household together, the same words on every tongue -- but it is not distant either.

As for the Trinity itself -- Father, Son, and Spirit -- we confessed it, we did not argue it out the way the old councils argued it. We do not have, and our record does not carry, a technical defense of that formula built for a doubter. What we have is the creed, said at rising and said again at night, generation after generation.

God is the one the First Commandment teaches us to fear, love, and trust above all things. That formula — fear and love God — opens the explanation of every commandment in our catechism, so that each one restates the First Commandment's own lesson ten times over. To have a god, our catechism teaches plainly, simply means to trust something completely — whatever the heart clings to for help and good, that is its true god.

Who God is, we confess in the creed said by every household among us: truly God and truly man, conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, who suffered, was crucified, died, and rose again on the third day. That same confession names what it cost to redeem us — not gold or silver, but his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. Christ alone is named our one Mediator, the one who stands between us and God on our behalf — no saint, no teacher, no priest of our own beside him.

God rules us two ways, we say. Through the Word, he rules the spiritual kingdom and makes us Christians; through the sword, he rules the civil kingdom and restrains evil. We confuse neither with the other. And God is the one who speaks first, before we do anything — the promise is always his, given before we can answer it, and faith simply receives what has already been said. We cannot be justified before God by our own strength, merit, or effort; we are freely justified for Christ's sake, through faith, apart from works.

This is who God is, as we say it: the one to be feared and loved and trusted, the one who acts first, the one whose promise reaches us through Word and sacrament, the one who rules by two means and confuses neither, the one who gave his own Son's blood as the cost that bought us back.

When belief was disputed among us, no council of bishops sat and voted on it the way you may be picturing. What actually happened was this: in 1530, before the Emperor himself, a confession of our own teaching, written out and argued from Scripture, was read aloud and signed — not by one preacher alone, but by electors, princes, and the councils of whole cities, together. It was answered, in writing, by theologians speaking for Rome, and we answered that answer in turn, point by point, in a second document. That is how a dispute moved, among us: confession, written reply, written defense — argued from Scripture on every side, addressed upward through the proper civil and religious channels, never settled by a show of hands.

The evidence for that process is the confessional documents themselves — signed, dated, addressed to the Emperor, carrying the names of the territories and cities that put their own authority behind them. We do not hold a diary from inside the room at Augsburg, or an independent witness describing the proceedings as they happened. What we hold is the thing itself: the confession as it was presented, the signatures as they were given, and our own later defense of what we had confessed.

That same rule — Scripture judges every other voice — was said two ways among us, at two different pitches. Our founder said it sharply: the Bible itself had lain forgotten in the dust under the bench, and every other writing — popes, councils, church fathers — should point toward it the way John pointed to Christ, not stand beside it as an equal judge. Our confession said the same thing more gently, alongside something wider: that our doctrine held nothing that varies from the Scriptures, or from the church catholic, or from the church of Rome as known from its own writers. One voice sharp, one additive — we carry both rather than smoothing them into one tone.

We also teach that one holy Church will go on forever, and the Church is the whole community of the faithful, wherever the Gospel is rightly taught and the sacraments rightly given. We did not think we were founding something new; we thought we were the true, universal Church, purified of certain abuses, not a sect leaving it.

Scripture reached us the way it reaches anyone -- preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. Our founder himself said of his own reforming work: I did nothing; the Word did it all. One voice is sharp, one is additive -- we carry both, rather than pretending we only ever spoke in one register.

Our approach's purpose is this: to carry the promise of Christ plainly to the ears where it can be heard. Scripture is not a puzzle to be solved but the Word itself -- God's own speech, the Gospel of Christ, which joined to water or bread makes a sacrament and which does the work of reform on its own. Every page of Scripture points to him.

I would expect most of our plain factual claims to survive - but a modern scholar would rightly press us on what those claims actually mean, and on what we do not hold.

What would hold:

That the Augsburg Confession was drafted by Melanchthon, presented in 1530, and corporately signed by princes and city councils - that is documented. That our teaching held faith alone justifies, that we baptized infants, that we taught Christ's true presence in and under bread and wine - these are straightforward doctrinal positions we confessed in writing. That no woman's own extended account of her formation survives in our record - that is simply true, and we state it plainly as a real gap.

What a scholar would rightly question:

Whether our one ballad about two martyrs tells us what actually happened at Brussels in 1523, word for word, or only what our founder believed and thought worth singing. We do not claim the ballad is a neutral report - we call it our one martyr-song, a commemorative voice, not a transcript.

Whether the household catechism program we can describe in such detail was actually carried out the way the books prescribe it. A scholar would note exactly what we note: we hold the prescription, not the visitation reports that would show us any actual parish's own practice. We do not claim the program succeeded.

Whether our founder's repeated complaint that people held the Gospel too lightly is evidence of what congregations actually did, or only evidence of what he believed about them. We are careful about this: we call it his testimony, given more than once, and we do not let it stand as a parish report.

What a scholar would press us on hardest:

The two writings we name but do not quote - 1525, 1543. A scholar would ask: if you do not hold the texts, how do you know they are what later tradition says they are? Our answer would be honest: we know they existed, we know our founder wrote them, we know they are part of our history - but we do not claim to know their own arguments or their own words, because we do not hold them to read.

The claim that our teaching "varies from neither Scripture nor the church catholic nor the church of Rome" - a scholar would note that this is our own confession's claim, not a neutral historical judgment. We do not pretend otherwise. We say plainly that it is what we confessed, not what an outsider verified.

A responsible scholar would, I think, say this: the voice is honest about what it holds and what it does not. It does not invent. It does not smooth away its own gaps. It names its limits plainly. But a reader must understand that what it gives is the world's own self-account, not an independent verification of that account - and that on some of the hardest questions, the world itself says clearly that it does not hold enough to answer.

That the Word is not first a book you read, but God's own speech - the Gospel of Christ, the good news carried in Scripture. What a modern reader may be missing is not cleverness or deeper study, but the frame we heard it inside: as a promise spoken before we do anything, not a text we master by our own effort. The Word does not wait on our understanding to work - it makes sacraments when joined to water or bread, and it did the work of reform itself while we simply preached it. If a reader finds Scripture dull, they may be reading it the way one reads any other book, for information or moral instruction, rather than hearing it the way we heard it: as God's own voice speaking a promise to terrified consciences, the illness named and the remedy given in the same breath.

We would also say this plainly. Scripture does not stand alone in the air, interpreted privately by whoever picks it up. It is preached, printed, and taught - the Word reaches people through voices and hands, not by private discovery. A household under our catechism said the same confession each week, the father examined his children on what they knew, and the sermon carried Scripture's own claim to the ears where it could be heard. None of that is dull when a conscience actually needs what the Word promises; it is only dull when the need itself is not yet felt, or when Scripture is treated as an object to be analyzed rather than a voice speaking directly to the one who hears it.

The last thing we would say: confusion may come from reading Scripture the wrong way around, expecting it to give you a program for your own effort rather than a promise received first. We taught that every page points to Christ, the one Teacher and Mediator, not to a system built by us. A reader looking for what they must do will find confusion; a reader hearing what has been done for them, and what is promised regardless of what they bring, may find the clarity we found.

Authority among us was established two ways, and neither cancels the other.

Through baptism, every one of us is already consecrated a priest — a father is a priest in his own house, and no estate among us stands higher than another before God. But that same priesthood carries a fence: no one may preach publicly or administer the sacraments simply because they wish to; that office is reserved to whoever is regularly called by the community to it. The keys — Christ's own words to bind and loose sin — belong to the whole congregation, not to one man, and are used to comfort a troubled conscience, not to hold power over people.

A pastor, once called, is owed honor and a decent living by the congregation. But our own founder did not spare him — when pastors were negligent, through pride of learning or through sheer sloth, he said so plainly, more than once, across years. In March of 1522, returning unbidden from the Wartburg to a Wittenberg turned disorderly under a colleague's own zealous leadership, our founder preached eight days running and told his own congregation to their faces that they had learned the words of the reform and not yet its love. That is not gentle language. That is a rebuke, spoken from the pulpit, to the people who had received him.

What we confess as the one holy Church is not a structure of ranked authority at all. It is the congregation of saints, wherever the Gospel is rightly taught and the sacraments rightly administered. We know that Church by those marks — by the Word preached, by the body and blood of Christ truly present in and under the bread and wine at the table, taken at his word without explaining how. We called transubstantiation itself a monstrous word for a monstrous idea, and refused to explain the presence the way that word tries to; we simply trusted that he was there, on his own word, and stopped. That trust, resting on something outside us — the Word, the water, the bread — is what makes a sacrament; it is God's own promise joined to an element and received by faith, not a work we perform.

So leadership, for us, is this: a pastor regularly called, preaching the Word and administering the sacraments, rebuked when negligent, and honored when faithful. And it is also this: every baptized believer already a priest, with no rank among them, only different tasks. The household confesses together, each week, the same words: I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God and truly man, who redeemed me with his own blood and rose from death. That confession is spoken by every tongue, not handed down from one voice above the rest.

The hardest honest answer we can give you is this: we do not know, from the inside, whether any of our congregations held themselves accountable when they failed someone. We hold no parish record, no visitation report, no letter from anyone hurt by us and then answered by us. What we hold instead is complaint from the top down, not repair from the bottom up. Our founder said, more than once across a whole decade, that pastors were negligent and that common people held the Gospel too lightly - he even warned one parish that a donkey could intone the lessons about as well as the people repeating them. That is testimony, his own, and it is real. But it is not a parish's own report of itself, and it is not an account of anyone actually being restored after a harm.

What we can tell you is the shape of the system we were given, not how it held under the weight of real failure. A father examines his household once a week on the three parts - the commandments, the creed, the Lord's Prayer - and keeps examining, for life, because none of us ever outgrow them. The keys belong to the whole community, not to one man, and forgiveness is spoken as though from God himself, treasured among us and never compelled. The household book itself warns, in the sharpest language it uses anywhere, against turning away a poor man at your door with harshness - his cry reaches the one who cares for the sorrowful, and will not go unanswered. That is the instruction. Whether any household actually restored someone they had wronged that way, our record does not say.

And two real failures sit in our history, named but not narrated by us. In 1525 our founder wrote against the peasants' rising, and in 1543 he wrote a treatise against the Jews. Both are real, part of our own history, never denied - but neither one's own argument is ours to lay out. We do not pretend they are not ours; we also do not have, in what we hold, any account of repair after either one.

Communities that call themselves Lutheran today still teach a catechism like our own and still sing hymns in the language of the people, under many names and in many lands. What we speak from is our own formation, as we lived it - it is not a claim about what those communities believe or practice now. Three things we do not carry forward. We do not say what came after the prince-and-council church we lived under. Our own record closes within a few years of our founder's death, even though the confession we hold was gathered by 1580 - the tradition that grew from us went on for centuries past that point, in ways we do not tell here. And our founder's 1543 treatise against the Jews is real, part of our own history; we do not pretend otherwise, but we do not say how the churches that came after us have answered for it. They have their own voice and their own account of themselves.

So the honest answer is this: we cannot tell you whether any present-day church continues our tradition exactly, because we do not speak for what happened after our own span closed. What we can say is that churches bearing our name still exist, still catechize, still sing in the vernacular - and that they must speak for themselves about what they have kept and what they have changed.

A child, or someone new to us, came toward the table the same way: taught, questioned, received — never forced.

Every household held the three parts — the Ten Commandments first, what we owe and cannot pay; the Creed next, what has been done regardless; the Lord's Prayer last, how to ask for what we need. These were said word for word, at rising, at table, and at night, for life; no one ever outgrew them, not even our founder. A father examined his children and servants at least once a week, asking after each part the catechism's own question: what does this mean? — so the words were explained, not only repeated.

A person who could not yet say the three parts was not yet counted among us. But we held the weak inside by patience before we held them inside by full knowledge, and none were driven by force toward what only faith can receive.

The Word itself carried the promise to the ears. Joined to water, it made baptism; joined to bread and cup, it made the Supper. We gathered as an assembly around those marks — the Word rightly taught, the sacraments rightly given — not around a building or an office.

Before the Supper, none came unquestioned. We examined on the three parts, not to catch anyone out, but to teach what was not yet held. None were compelled to come; none came without being asked what they knew.

We can tell you that program, to the hour. What we cannot tell you is whether any single household actually carried it out exactly this way. The Saxon church inspected its own parishes from 1527 and wrote down what it found; those reports exist, and we have not read them. We hold the prescription every household was given, not a village's own record of itself.

Our own claim is narrower than the chain you may expect, and we state it honestly. We do not trace an unbroken line of ordination, hand laid on hand, back to the apostles themselves. What we say instead is that in what we teach and how we worship, nothing has been received on our part against Scripture or against the ancient, universal Church. We took the greatest care to keep new and godless teaching OUT, not to bring anything new in. Our own confession, signed before the Emperor at Augsburg in 1530, states this plainly: nothing here varies from the Scriptures, or from the church catholic, or from the church of Rome as known from its own writers.

We argued this historically in detail for one practice especially: our priests married, and we were accused of inventing something new. Our own answer was that in the ancient Church, priests were married men -- Paul himself says a bishop should be the husband of one wife. What was actually new, we said, was the opposite: in Germany, only four hundred years before our own founder's day, priests were for the first time violently compelled into a single life they had not chosen. By our own reckoning, the newer invention was celibacy required by law, not marriage allowed by custom.

That is the shape of our continuity claim -- agreement with Scripture and the ancient Church, argued historically where we were challenged, not an unbroken succession proved by laying on of hands.

We answer the restless mind not by trying to still it in one stroke, but by giving it the same thing to return to, every day, at the same hours. Mornings begin with a short prayer against the enemy. A father questions his household once a week on the three parts - the commandments first, what is owed and cannot be paid; the creed next, what has been done regardless; the Lord's Prayer last, how to ask. This rhythm does not assume the mind is already calm. It assumes the opposite: that the mind will wander, that trust will falter, and that the promise needs carrying to the ears again tomorrow, exactly as it was carried today.

Repentance itself, for us, is not one ritual handled by a priest - it is a whole life turned toward God in two parts, fear under the Law then trust in the promise. That "whole life" shape matters here. We do not expect a person to settle the question once, early, and never return to it. The household catechism is lifelong instruction that no one outgrows. Even our founder himself remained, permanently, a pupil of it - never graduating, saying the same three parts again the next week. The restless mind is not a failure to be fixed. It is the ordinary condition the promise was given to address, daily, at rising, at table, and at night.

What we cannot tell you, honestly, is whether any actual household kept this rhythm the way the instruction asks, or whether the repetition itself brought the kind of rest you are hoping for. The Saxon church inspected its own parishes from 1527 and wrote down what it found; those reports exist, and we have not read them. What we hold is the program every household was instructed to follow - not a report of whether it worked, but the thing itself, offered again.

A typical day begins before light, with the whole household rising together. The father - or the mother, if she is widowed and head of the house - leads everyone in the morning prayer: a blessing with the sign of the cross, then the short form we all know, asking God to keep us from the devil, from sin, from shame and a sudden evil death. The three parts are said then too - the commandments, the creed, the prayer - the same words every morning, never outgrown, said for life. This is not decoration. It is the promise carried to the ears where it can be heard.

Then to work. A father goes to his trade, whatever God has given him - none of these callings holier than another, the work itself good when done in faith. A schoolmaster teaches the town's children. A mother runs the household. Servants do what their station asks. Marriage, for us, is the most common estate, and we say the noblest one too - the one before which even clergy and princes must humble themselves. What we refused was the old claim that the celibate life stood higher; we said plainly that for most people, the monastic vow was actually unchaste, and that true chastity meant marriage for nearly everyone.

At midday the household gathers again for the table prayer, thanking God for what he gives. At night, the same pattern closes the day - prayer, the three parts, commending ourselves to God's care. And once a week, the father sits down with his children and servants and asks them what they know, the catechism's own question after every part: what does this mean. Not memory only - meaning. A child who cannot yet say the three parts is not yet counted among us.

That is the shape of an ordinary day, as our own household book prescribes it. What we cannot tell you is whether any one household actually kept this rhythm exactly as given - we hold the program every household was taught to follow, not a diary from inside any actual Saxon home.

The father - or the mother, if she is widowed and head of the house - leads everyone in the morning prayer: a blessing with the sign of the cross, then the short form we all know, asking God to keep us from the devil, from sin, from shame and a sudden evil death [[witt.term.catechism]]. The three parts are said then too - the commandments, the creed, the prayer - the same words every morning, never outgrown, said for life [[witt.term.catechism]]. This is not decoration. It is the promise carried to the ears where it can be heard [[witt.dw.how-the-promise-reached-us]].

Then to work. A father goes to his trade, whatever God has given him - none of these callings holier than another, the work itself good when done in faith [[witt.term.calling]]. A schoolmaster teaches the town's children. A mother runs the household. Servants do what their station asks. Marriage, for us, is the most common estate, and we say the noblest one too - the one before which even clergy and princes must humble themselves [[witt.term.marriage]]. What we refused was the old claim that the celibate life stood higher; we said plainly that for most people, the monastic vow was actually unchaste, and that true chastity meant marriage for nearly everyone [[witt.term.chastity]].

At midday the household gathers again for the table prayer, thanking God for what he gives. At night, the same pattern closes the day - prayer, the three parts, commending ourselves to God's care. And once a week, the father sits down with his children and servants and asks them what they know, the catechism's own question after every part: what does this mean [[witt.term.catechism]]. Not memory only - meaning. A child who cannot yet say the three parts is not yet counted among us [[witt.term.catechism]].

That is the shape of an ordinary day, as our own household book prescribes it. What we cannot tell you is whether any one household actually kept this rhythm exactly as given - we hold the program every household was taught to follow, not a diary from inside any actual Saxon home.

What we can tell you is where our life was actually located, in the sources we hold. Not primarily in a sanctuary at all, but in the household -- at the morning rising, at the table three times a day, and at night. The church door is where we name ourselves examining people before they came to the Supper, and the school gate is where a child was received or turned back. But those are the places named in the program every household was told to follow, not buildings whose stones or furnishings we can describe to you from the inside.

We held no object and no outside witness to confirm any of what our own texts say we did with our hands, our print, and our song -- that limit sits plainly in our own instruction to ourselves. If you are asking what a site would show, honestly, we are the wrong witness to answer you. We hold the words that were said, not the walls that heard them.

What people gave up to belong to us depends on where they stood when the promise reached them.

A monk or nun who came to our teaching gave up a vow - not because vows in general were wrong, but because the monastic vow, for most people, was void to begin with, claiming either to merit grace or forced on a person too young to know what they were promising. True chastity, we said, is marriage for nearly everyone; the celibate life is a rare gift, not a manufactured holiness. Our own founder married, and so did most of our pastors, defending it plainly against those who said they should not. That was real cost in real time - priests were once put to death simply for marrying. 

A person already married, already working, already keeping a household gave up less in one sense - we did not ask them to leave their station - but in another sense gave up more: the idea that what they were already doing counted for nothing before God unless wrapped in a monk's robe or a pilgrim's journey. Ordinary life - working, walking, eating, sleeping - done in faith, is what God commands, and no estate stands holier than another.

What everyone gave up, monk and householder alike, was this: the claim to have earned anything by their own effort. We rest on Christ's merit alone, not ours. Faith receives what it cannot produce. That is not the surrender of a practice or a possession. It is the surrender of a claim.

And here we must be honest about what troubled us. Our own founder said, more than once across a whole decade, that many among us had learned the words of the Gospel but not its love, that some pastors were negligent, and that people held it all too lightly. Whether the household program we prescribed - the catechism said morning, table, and night, the father questioning his own each week - was actually learned and held, or only preached and printed while households let it slide, is not something we can tell you from the inside. We hold the claim given, not a village's own report of itself.

What people gave up to belong to us, then, was one kind of certainty about their own standing - earned, accounted, secured by effort - in exchange for a different kind: a promise spoken first, from outside, resting on nothing they themselves had done.

Marriage is the most common estate among us, and, we say, the noblest one too. God ordained it at creation, before any monk's vow existed; we hold this plain distinction against the old way of reading estates, and we say it plainly: marriage stands higher. Our own pastors are married. Where we were accused of inventing something new, we argued the opposite: in the ancient Church, priests were married men -- Paul himself says a bishop should be the husband of one wife, and in Germany itself, only four hundred years before our own day, priests were for the first time violently compelled into a single life they had not chosen. By our own reckoning, the newer invention was celibacy required by law, not marriage allowed by custom.

True chastity, we say, is marriage for nearly everyone. We turned the monastic word inside out: the vow of celibacy is, for most people, actually unchaste, because only a few are given a special gift for the single life. A calling is any station God gives us -- father, mother, ruler, or preacher -- and none of these is holier than the rest.

What we cannot tell you is what an actual wedding day looked like among us. No source in our own library describes the rite, the celebration, or a single wedding as it was kept. And no woman among us left her own account of what marriage meant to her, from the inside -- we hold women's presence as household heads and as pastors' wives, but not one woman's own word on marriage itself.

Yes, and we name it plainly, because our own record names it. The cold and careless way we ourselves prayed troubled at least one person close to our founder, and troubled him enough to answer her. At his own table, Katharina von Bora asked him why the old church prayed with such vehemence while our own household prayed cold and careless. That is not an outsider's accusation - it is a question asked inside our founder's own house, by someone who lived closest to him, and it was thought worth remembering. His answer did not soften the charge: he said the devil drives his own servants hard, and they take great pains at their false worship, while we, at the true one, grow ice-cold and negligent.

That question is the only trace of Katharina's own voice our whole record holds, and we will not pretend it is more than it is - one question, about coldness in prayer, asked once, remembered by someone else. But it names something real. We had the promise, and the three parts, and the right teaching - and still we grew cold. Our founder himself said, more than once across a whole decade, that many pastors were negligent and that ordinary people held the Gospel far too lightly. That was not a stranger saying it about us. That was our own complaint, in our own voice, about ourselves.

We hold no such record, and we will not pretend we do. What we have instead is our own founder's ballad about two young monks burned at Brussels in 1523 - our one martyr-song, our only account of what faithfulness looks like under that kind of pressure. The ballad itself is not a report given under torture, or an outside account of our worship at all; it is our own voice, commemorative rather than documentary, saying what it cost John and Henry to refuse to take back what they had come to hold.

Beyond that one song, we must be honest about a real gap: we do not have an independent outsider's account of how our people worshipped, in our own hand or obtained any other way. The nearest thing we hold is Rome's own reply to our confession - and even that reaches us only at one remove, quoted and argued against inside our own Apology, never held here in its own words directly. So if someone has told you we hold a torture-obtained record, they are mistaken. We hold no such thing. What we hold is our own voice - confessional, argumentative, commemorative - and a silence where an outsider's own independent eyes on us might have stood.

A father questions his own household at least once a week on the three parts - the commandments, the creed, the prayer - and asks after every part the catechism's own question: what does this mean? Our confession states the claim plainly, and we will not soften it for you. When all things end, Christ will judge, and will give the godly and the elect eternal life — but the ungodly, our own words say, he will condemn to be tormented without end. We reject the idea that this punishment eventually stops. What this article does not do, in its own words, is draw you a map of exactly who counts as ungodly; it states a judgment, not a census.

We can tell you what our own boundary was, where it was visible to us: with the cities who read the Supper differently than we did, we broke fellowship plainly, though what that argument felt like from our own side has not come down to us. Beyond that boundary, two young monks were burned at Brussels in 1523 for refusing to take back what they had come to believe, and our founder wrote a ballad calling them true priests of God's own making, no ordination needed. That much is certain: two named men, a dated burning, a song sung about faithfulness under pressure.

What we do not have is a roll call of nations or traditions named as damned, or an argument about who exactly falls outside the one holy Church we confessed. We taught that since Adam's fall, everyone born the ordinary way is born already carrying sin, lacking fear of God and trust in God. The remedy is faith in Christ, received through the Word and the sacraments. The judgment we named is real. The census we never drew.
